text: The industry is in a tailspin.
There are fewer opportunities for writers and producers and people who make things.
And I really had the conviction that AI can help you figure out who you are, how you have to survive in this world, and also how to make things that will then promote you and promote your career.
Depending on who you ask, right now is an apocalypse for creative people, or it's like the best time to be alive ever.
I think it's one of the most important questions about AI as a technology.
Can you use it to make good art, or can you only use it to make slop?
That's why I'm extremely excited for this episode.
My co-host, Natalia Quintero, interviewed Fred Graver.
Fred is a four-time Emmy Award-winning filmmaker and technologist who,
is using AI all the time to make really great stuff in film.
And he came on to share how he uses it, how it can be used as a creative tool, and the dirty secret in Hollywood that a lot of people use it even if they won't admit to it.
So, Natalia, tell us about the conversation.
Yeah.
It was so cool to talk to Fred and to learn from someone who's been a leader at the top of their industry for so many decades.
And what's interesting is that Fred has actually done this a few times.
He started his career as a Disney Imagineer.
That's the coolest thing.
Kind of the dream job.
And then he built this incredible career at VH1 and MTV.
And then he kind of threw it all away and became the head of TV at Twitter when it was a startup.
And that didn't totally make sense.
But he had this really interesting thesis of wanting to get closer and closer to the audience.
And now he's done it again.
He's basically built what
We'll be compound producing and rebuild the production process from the ground up using his decades of expertise as an Emmy Award winning artist to do it all over again.
And we all get to use his skills.
So if you want to be a producer, now you can produce like Fred.
I love it.
It's a great episode.
Let's dive in.

And I would understand, no, that's the joke.

So that's, yes, that's how I got started.

you know, the whole kind of, you're going to get replaced by somebody who knows how to use AI.

It was a great gig.

In the 70s, Norman was the king of television.

And he was doing some new things with television.
And I got hired.
I worked with him.
It was an incredible learning experience, which then translated into my being a comedy writer.
And I worked for Cheers and In Living Color.
And then I heard a modem.

Everything's going to be on something on your desk, and you're going to be able to do everything yourself.
Um...
And so my first kind of tech gig was I was working with the Disney Imagineers.
And there was this effort back in the day.
It was Mike Ovitz and Jeffrey Katzenberg and those guys.
And they were terrified.
This was like the late 90s, early 2000s.
They were terrified by the Internet.
But, you know, they began putting real bets down on what is this thing going to be.
So I was...
and I was at MTV Networks in the kind of early web days.
And then I took another right turn.
I got hired by Twitter.
This would be late 2000s, right?
It's like the second year that Twitter was around.
And the theory was if famous people that people love, celebrities or TV shows, are on Twitter, then people will get on Twitter.
And that's the best advertising we could do.
And so that was my job, was to get the bird and real use cases onto the screen.
Probably best case...
that ever happened was the famous Ellen DeGeneres selfie.
Blew up, but that was how many million dollars worth of advertising.
So I did that.
And then I was doing some consulting and things, and somebody said to me, hey, there's this machine learning thing that,
that's AI and the engineers don't understand how people talk and people don't know what to talk about when they get to the machine.
And so I became a conversation designer at Microsoft.
I was literally scripting bots and I was working with the AI teams and it
It was weirdly fascinating because you're just dealing with what's going to become AI, what's going to become this interface, and trying to figure out what will that conversation be.
And also, it is a conversation.
I think what a lot of people, when they freak out about AI, and they freak out about an enormous box of things instead of all the things that are inside, but they're kind of like...
They use it as a search engine, or it gave me the wrong... And they don't realize, no, it's a relationship.
I was doing that.
I was writing... Then they moved me to writing presentations.
Microsoft's great kind of secret sauce is they have decades of data about how people use their software and what they realized they really needed to do.
So if you're United Airlines and people are calling in to do whatever they're going to do, can we have...
an AI bot, can we have co-pilot go through everything we already know from 30 years of you guys using software to help them solve their problem.

And so I did that for quite a while, writing these presentations, saying, here's what AI is and here's what it does and here's your problems and the solution to your problems, oddly enough, are Microsoft products.
Of course they are.
Of course they were.

What's so interesting to me about your career though is that at every sort of major turning point you kind of, you have turned towards technology as early as joining the Disney Imagineers which at the time was revolutionary and the work that they did has been so revolutionary.
What do you think has been the core insight that you've taken at every turn, like from the Imagineers to, you know, you worked in like the golden era of TV.
Yeah.
But you also turned from that to go to Twitter, which must have been a bold move.
Like there must have been sort of like a key insight that led there.
But like what have been the key insights and those different pivot points?
There's two answers.
One is the real answer, which reveals me to be a terribly shallow person.
Sometimes you look at something and you just go, I want in.
And for me, growing up, I grew up on the south side of Chicago, and I watched way too much television.
And all I thought to myself is, I want to be on the other side of that screen.
I want in.
So it's I want in there.
It's I want in because there's some very funny people doing stuff here.
And I like funny people, and I get along with them really well.
I want in.
The technology turn for me, again, I hear a modem, and this was in the days of like CompuServe, and there's no browser, there's nothing, it's just easy.
But the first thing I joined was the whole Earth electronic link, the well.

It was Chloe Sladden and Dick Costolo.

It'll just be fun.
It'll be really great.
And so there was that.
But still, once I saw...
what AI was capable of, it was like, yeah, I want in.

My old tribe is not thrilled with the prospect of what this is going to be or what it might mean.
And yet there's a new
group of people, which I want to be very careful, it's not defined by age.
It's defined by a sensibility and a mindset.
There's a new group of people who are storytellers and who are in what I still call show business because they don't think like David Ellison.
They think like people like, let's get a...
blanket and a garage and put on something.

Or how can I do this with Google Story Studio?
Or how can I do, oh wait, this is really interesting.
And then they begin kind of getting in and playing with it.
And those people, to me, that's the group where I go like, okay, I want in, or at this point, I really do feel like, okay,
I might be one of the first kind of settlers.
If there was one key insight that you took away from working early on with like the Imagineers, like what might have that been?
The Imagineers were founded by Disney to help him build stuff in the theme parks.
And anytime new technology came around, the Imagineers, a group of the Imagineers would be assigned to figure out what does that mean to us?
The most threatening thing in the late 90s for Disney was that technology was going to give the audience unprecedented access to IP.
That you could suddenly digitize a copyright, you could take Snow White and the Seven Dwarves and let your imagination run free and this is terrifying.
At the same time, you could also see that the audience is going to be in this new place and they're going to want to have access to that stuff.
So the insight was suddenly there was a brand new tension.
There was a new tension between what
the audience and creators would have access to and be able to make versus what you were able to make given the moat around your business and the barbarians were building bridges over the moat.
So fast forwarding to MTV, VH1, and the work that you did there, what do you think might have been your key takeaway then having worked in the golden era of television?
Yeah.
So the key takeaway for me, again, was open it up to the audience.
And that's your survival.
And what does that mean?
So for example...
I created a show called Best Week Ever, and it was doing very well.
And we had created a Tumblr just for the producers to talk to each other.
And we realized suddenly that there were 10 or 15,000 people reading our Tumblr.
And it literally was just like, read the audience signal, see what's going on.
And it was a complete accident.
That's so interesting because it then sounds like your move to Twitter was kind of like further embracing the audience, right?
Like moving.
It almost seems like at every point in your career you've taken a step closer to the audience.
I think that's really true.
And I think...
What is great about AI, so you're talking about kind of codifying things.
If you start out as a writer and you want to use AI, I have kind of a few things that I kind of say you should do.
You should create a who I am as a writer document.
And you should throw in your inspirations, what you love, what you read, what you aspire to do, all of that.
And then you also have a document that this is the thing I'm working on.
Right?
And it could be... And by the way, you don't even need to be specific about...
I have this idea.
I have this thing that I really, really, really want to kind of get at.
I want to think about.
In the same kind of way that like Joan Didion once said, I don't know what I think about something until I write about it.
I have this thing I want to explore.
And AI is great at that.
And then you go... You begin...
putting as much as you know about that thing in.
And the first thing you can say to AI is, does this idea and this person that I'm describing have anything to do with each other?
Right?
And then you kind of play around with that.
And the third question is, who's out there?
Is there an audience out there for this thing?
What platforms are they on?
How do they consume media?
What are the questions they care about that relate to the thing I'm writing or even bigger questions that they care about?
Somebody in the Atlantic did this, I think.
They created the focus group for something.
And you could actually literally do that.

Like create a focus group of eight people from a range where there's a guy over here who's the guy you really wish you hadn't invited into the focus group because he's really negative and you have somebody who really loves what you're doing.
And begin working on the idea that you're working on to get feedback.
And so none of that is about AI writing for you.
Everything is about having AI as kind of a virtual writer's room, as a group of intelligences that can help you think through things.
So referencing Compound Writing, which is a great plug-in that Katy Perry on our own built.
Yeah, give her all the credit she can get.
Which I'm a big fan of Katy.
She's fantastic.
And that was built off of Kieran Claussen's
compound engineering plugin.

Right?

And so when I want to build a new product, I want to defer to experts in that field to
follow the steps that they would take in order to build a product so that I'm doing it safely and following best practices.
The same for writing, right?
Katie has codified at least her approach to writing the kind of writing that she does.

Can you speak a little bit more about that?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
So think about
There's a kind of core that exists, and what you pour into that core are two different things.
One is expertise around, so in my case, it's expertise around creating entertainment product.
And there is a fair amount of product design and product management that goes into this.
And you get the expertise of everybody.

You could go into everybody from David O. Selznick to Francis Coppola to Quentin Tarantino to all the way down the line.
There's all the expertise.
It goes around writing, it goes around producing, it goes around editing, it goes around marketing and distribution.
There's even people who are just really brilliant who are just like business operations and legal people.
And there's this, you can put all of that and I'm building that where I kind of like going in and going like,
You're going to make 1,001 decisions in the next week, probably.
So half of this is, here's the experts, right?
And that AI has ingested all this, thought about it.
And if you're going, okay, the marketing people and the writers are disagreeing.
Right?
The writer thinks these characters are answering these questions and the marketing people say, I can't sell that.
Right?
Well, what are other ways people have solved those issues?
Just to give you advice, just to suggest, or kind of like help you mediate that, which by the way, also results in less friction because so much of this in show business gets personal,
People get in a huff, they walk away, they have horrible fights.
The best part about this is when the movie comes out or the TV series premieres, everybody's patting themselves on the back, oh, we made it despite this.
I'm like, stop, you didn't have to do it in the first place.
The other half though, is also your personal culture.
So if you're a production company or a studio, you have a way of doing things and thinking about things.
And you can put that into the hub of the AI central core as well.
And everybody who's part of the process has already also said, here's a document about who I am.
Here's what my career is all about.
Here's the kind of way I work.
And so now you've got this kind of really great Petri dish.
of cultural documents that AI can help you think through.
And the last thing I'll say is, people in show business still make things the way Henry Ford made cars.
There's this assembly line.
And if you say to them, no, make it a circle.
So by the way, the marketing and business people are talking to the writer and the pre-production people now.
before you start making decisions that get locked in or whatever.
Sometimes the production company has got 10 people, 15 people.
Sometimes it's a writer who at this point is the entire team.
Right.

Which is...
It's the only thing that AI can do really well.
It's like follow directions clearly.

So what I love about, again, like the engineering tools that or the plugins that our team has put out is that when it comes to engineering, I understand that there's basically like three steps to engineering.
And what Kieran has done is just kind of like codified what excellence looks like in those three steps.
First, you make a plan.
Um, there's all kinds of things involved with making a good plan.
So we'll follow the instructions on that.

It's kind of like that loop that you discussed.
What in its most basic form do you think is that loop for writing or producing in your case?
Yeah.
We'll break it into three steps.
There's ideation, and we'll call it architecture or design.
It is the thing that produces a script.
And that's the first thing, is you get something that is a written document that is the best embodiment of the idea you're trying to work on.
The next phase is production.
And it's everything from how do we prepare to make this thing?
And it's a very similar process whether you're working with a straight-on regular kind of movie or TV series or a hybrid series that uses some AI.
Or even in all – I'm working with a studio now, and we're making an AI animated series.
Yeah.

So there's this production process that's everything from pre-production considerations to keeping everybody going within the production.
And I would include editing in there as well.
And there's a lot of stuff in there.

There's storyboards, there's all the, you know, it's fascinating to me that Martin Scorsese is like one of the first people to kind of come out and go, oh, I'm working with this company that's using story, creating storyboards with AI.

Like, well, what about the storyboard artists?

You're going to have to get another job.
It's the mob.
So there's the production phase, and AI can help with that.
And then there's the how do you reach the audience with this thing phase.
How do you market and distribute this?
What's fascinating to me about having worked with a couple of production studios in Hollywood is,
is the marketing people are all in on figuring out how to use AI to the point where they will create a campaign for something and they work with companies that are doing it with AI.
They will watch intent to purchase a ticket or ticket purchases based on a trailer and they will rewrite the trailer almost on an hour by hour basis.
You go, OK, let's A-B test this, let's try this, let's try that.
And that, again, AI can be part of that process.
What I think is fascinating is, again, you make it a circle so that here's the ideation and design and architecture phase.
And it works.
Why not have the marketing people right away going, well, let's create a proxy trailer for that.
Let's see if we can sell tickets to that even though it doesn't exist yet, right?
Which is essentially what show business has always been about.
So those are the three phases, and that's where I think in every step, AI can speak to the people who are doing it and can inform the decisions that everybody's making.
